📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense. Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.

While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.

Sources indicate that before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.

In a recent development, asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the newly introduced Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.

Graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.

Asus will sell this device in two memory configurations (plus some lower-specced retailer-specific SKUs), but the one I’ve been testing (and the one that makes the most sense alongside the RTX Spark) has 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It supports up to 300GB/s of raw bandwidth, which is fast for shared system memory. However, using a dedicated GPU typically gets you higher throughput with a GDDR7 memory interface. Still, you get several times more memory than a gaming GPU in this machine.

Recent findings suggest that this is essentially an Nvidia Spark DGX workstation with a screen and keyboard. It also runs Windows 11, which lowers the barrier to entry if you want local AI agents. While many local AI setups focus on 27-billion-parameter models that will fit on a video card, the Asus ProArt P16 can easily load models with 100-plus billion parameters, with enough left over for lighter background AI tasks.

Industry observers note that nvidia and Asus say the Spark’s AI compute and ample memory are enough power to run frontier-level AI models locally. That means you can get powerful AI compute without running through your allotment of expensive tokens or sending all your data to a server in the cloud. Ignoring the AI angle, the ProArt P16 has to be a good laptop before it makes sense for even the most AI-obsessed buyers to consider it. Luckily, it gets all the basic laptop things right.

In a recent development, it’s nice to see a wide array of ports on this machine. There are three USB-C ports with USB4 support, and they’re split between the left and right sides. That makes connecting devices and charging much easier. There’s also a legacy USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 port, full HDMI, a 3.5 mm jack, and an SD card reader.

The machine comes with a beefy 140 W USB-C charger, which can get you a few hours of use in just a minute or two of charging. Asus says you can get up to 12 hours of use per charge, but that depends very much on what you’re doing. Watching video at low brightness might get you even more than 12 hours, but expect somewhat less for mixed use and even less for heavy AI workloads. In my (unscientific) testing, after a full workday and tinkering with AI on the side, the P16 usually has about 30 percent of its battery left.

The 16-inch 120Hz OLED display is overall very good, sporting a 4K+ resolution of 3840 x 2400. The stacked (tandem) pixels mean you get an incredibly high 1,600 nits of peak brightness. However, tandem OLEDs do tend to look a bit grainy with solid colors at lower brightness levels. I’ve laid eyes on two P16 units, one of which was noticeably more grainy than the other—so that’s something to look out for. However, the texture is easy to ignore at normal viewing distances and mid-to-high brightness.

The trackpad is enormous (150.3 x 99.5 mm) and relies on haptic clicks instead of a physical mechanism. This is a relatively new thing for Windows laptops, which are still catching up to Apple’s trackpads. That stated, the ProArt’s pad works very well. It’s appropriately sensitive, and you can adjust the click intensity and detection threshold.

In a recent development, the keyboard is a little on the narrow side for a larger laptop, but the keys feel great. There’s ample travel, the tactility is sharp, and the firm keyboard deck ensures no flex at the bottom of each keystroke. The aluminum chassis is overall very solid, but it only comes in white or black, with the latter being your only option for the high-end model. The matte case looks great, but it is a magnet for smudges (particularly the plastic of the keys).

Unlike previous ProArt laptops that had standard GPUs, there’s no dedicated memory for the RTX Spark’s graphics and AI cores. Windows sees the machine as having 64GB of system RAM and 64GB of video memory, but in reality, this shared 128GB of memory is adjusted dynamically based on what you’re doing.

Since this is a Windows machine, there is some overhead that limits your AI workloads. On a DGX Spark box with the same underlying hardware, all the memory is available for AI. Here, you’re capped at about 110GB. That’s still a huge amount of memory for AI, far surpassing what you can get on even the most expensive consumer-level GPUs.

There are a few clear advantages to making the ProArt P16 your AI hub. Running an AI model locally on the Spark’s Blackwell cores lets you keep all your data private. When you interact with ChatGPT or Gemini, your interactions and data become training and advertising fodder. You’re also trusting the AI provider to run your workloads on the right model, and they’ll often route requests to cheaper ones to save money.

With an RTX Spark laptop, you have total control over how the AI operates. That also means you have to do all the setup and management yourself. The ProArt comes with a few Asus apps, which will streamline setup for a subset of AI-powered tasks, but installing a third-party agent is where things get interesting (but not always good).

Sources indicate that nvidia’s laptop AI chip is optimized for desktop clients like OpenClaw and Hermes, allowing you to download the AI models of your choice in a fairly simple graphical UI. I tested various models in different size ranges. Asus recommends starting with Qwen 27B, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that splits the difference between size and efficiency. I also loaded a few versions of Google’s Gemma open models in the same size range.

But these are all small enough that you could run them on a high-end GPU. To push the Spark, I grabbed a few larger models like the Qwen Flash Next, a 90GB download with 125 billion parameters. This model occupies almost all the shared memory when active, whereas the smaller ones won’t even go beyond the GPU’s reserved 64GB.

According to recent reports, the nice (and scary) thing about setting up a local agent on Windows is that it can control the PC. Once the model is loaded in your preferred AI framework, you can just ask it to handle additional configuration. Need to set up access for your online accounts? Just ask. Manage installed tools and apps? Just ask. Surely nothing could go wrong, right?

In short order, I set up agent workflows to access and analyze data from test email accounts, manage local files, revision a coding project, and analyze the content of images in my photo library. I also used ComfyUI workflows to generate images and videos locally without worrying about running through a limited allotment of tokens in the cloud. I’ll admit, I don’t have much use for media generation, but some of these local image models have gotten surprisingly good. Of course, the machine itself is expensive enough that you could pay for the most extravagant AI intends for a few years before breaking even. Still, the data and compute are all yours.

Industry observers note that A few tragic tales about local agents nuking file directories or exposing data have made the rounds, and that’s a real concern when you start giving these things access to your PC—these models can do whatever you can do while sitting at the keyboard. I tested the P16’s AI capabilities with that in mind, ensuring I had no irreplaceable or sensitive data on the machine. Agents are supposed to seek authorization before taking action, but mistakes may happen, even if you’re being careful.

Industry observers note that the agents didn’t make any huge mistakes in my testing, but watching the chain of thought bounce around can be maddening, like an unguided robot vacuum bouncing into walls. But like a vacuum, today’s AI agents usually get to the right place.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, it does feel very futuristic. You give the machine a problem or tell it to troubleshoot something, and it does it without sharing any data with anyone. It’s a different way of using a PC. That’s cool, but it’s also not without frustration. Even though these models are often able to arrive at the correct result, they may not do so very swiftly.

During normal operation, the Asus ProArt P16 is whisper-quiet. As soon as you start running inference for AI, though, the fans kick into high gear. The machine absolutely burns through the enormous 100 Wh battery, which is the largest cell you can legally bring on an airplane in the US. You really only get about two hours of inference without the power cable, and you might not get as much done as you’d think in that time. For example, scanning a day’s emails and generating action items takes around five minutes with a mid-weight model.

With simple tasks, models like Qwen 27B can churn through 20 or so tokens per second (with default “medium” effort mode). That’s a bit slower than you’ll get with cloud-based frontier models, which are also more capable thanks to their powerful server hardware. As long as you don’t need to ask it if Taiwan is a country, Qwen seems like the best option for local AI currently. Google’s mid-weight Gemma models can occasionally hit up to 40 tokens per second, but that figure tends to come down to a quarter of that speed for more complex tasks.

While Qwen Flash Next does produce better results, it takes so long I usually stick with the smaller models—it chugs along at just a few tokens per second unless you drop its thinking level. You can still make use of all that RAM by running multiple concurrent agents, though. That may be the real promise of RTX Spark machines, but that requires you to have a lot of AI-powered projects in mind. If you’re just using a Spark laptop as an alternative to keeping a ChatGPT window open, you should probably pay for ChatGPT Pro instead of buying a $7,000 PC.

While the RTX Spark is aimed at AI workloads, it’s also an all-around speedy Windows platform. It is, however, an Arm-based chip with 20 Nvidia Grace CPU cores. Microsoft has a sordid history with Windows on Arm, but things are finally in a better place.

Sources indicate that the Windows Prism emulator can run x86 and x64 programs well enough that you won’t usually notice the difference, and some past software gaps, like Google Drive and VPN apps, have been addressed with native Arm versions. So you don’t need to fear Arm chips on Windows anymore unless you have very specific legacy software and hardware needs.

Sources indicate that in daily use, the ProArt P16 with RTX Spark is extremely responsive. It’s still usable even when you fill up the memory with AI agents running inference in the background. There are very few systems that directly compare to the RTX Spark right now, but here are some system benchmarks of the Asus ProArt P16.

Nvidia has pushed the idea that Spark can be your primary gaming machine, too. But here, emulation is more of a bother. There are virtually no native Arm games for Windows, and emulation takes a bite out of your performance. Titles that require system-level anti-cheat measures may not run because those cannot be emulated. However, Nvidia has made progress here, collaborating with some major vendors like Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, and Denuvo to support their technology on Spark. It’s still early, though, and you may encounter errors.

The GPU component of the Spark N1X is equivalent to the most powerful Blackwell-based gaming GPUs on the market, but emulation means performance won’t quite measure up. You also have to remember that the ProArt P16 has an incredibly high-resolution OLED screen. Running games at native resolution, even without the emulation overhead, is already pushing the limits of the hardware.

In a recent development, aside from the benchmark numbers, I put the ProArt P16 to work playing some games. While they ran well enough to play, it’s not as simple as cranking the settings to max like you would on an x86 system with a Blackwell GPU. For example, Baldur’s Gate 3 is not exactly a graphical tour de force, and it’s more CPU-bound than some other AAA games.

Industry observers note that I had to make some compromises to maintain 60 fps, even in less busy areas of the game. It was basically a trade-off between lowering detail and using aggressive DLSS or dropping the game below native resolution. You can expect Spark-based machines like this to run most games with high graphical settings, but ultra settings will be out of reach if you want to maintain good frame rates.

In a purely technical way, it’s cool that you can run powerful 100GB AI models on a laptop. Devices like the DGX Spark and DIY GPU clusters can perform similar tasks, but having everything centralized on one machine makes it more appealing as a way to get things done with AI, and Windows makes it easy to get started.

It has been revealed that the ProArt P16 can be your one and only computer, handling gaming, productivity, and AI inference. However, it can be hard to really take advantage of all the AI capabilities of the machine. You’re looking at running either one or two large, powerful agents at very slow speeds or a collection of smaller models much faster. That means you need to have plenty of AI applications in mind. Otherwise, you might as well get a standard laptop.

You probably already know if that’s something you want. The kind of person running multiple concurrent agentic tasks using cloud systems might benefit from a PC like the ProArt P16, and in some extreme instances, they might want to spend $7,000 on the machine with 128GB of RAM. However, you could also step down to the 64GB model to save a few thousand dollars and still get some useful AI capabilities as models get more efficient.

Recent findings suggest that the Asus ProArt P16 is really a niche machine. If you want something primarily for gaming, an x86 system with a discrete GPU makes more sense, and a lighter, productivity-focused laptop is better for most buyers. The ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of how a local AI-powered future could work, but it’s not a good purchase for anyone but the most fervent AI boosters right now.

Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO, board chair

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The reinstatement, unveiled Monday morning, is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr.
  • Sources indicate that that assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia’s board of directors has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and chairman of the board, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of multiple scandals.

The reinstatement, unveiled Monday morning, is “effective immediately” and was based in part on “input from senior levels of the United States government” that assured the board members that “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Sources indicate that that assurance comes despite Huang’s admitted affair with a woman who, US intelligence sources believe, was working as a Chinese spy and allegations that Nvidia had subverted export controls meant to keep Nvidia chips from reaching China. It also comes despite multiple developing investigations from multiple different government departments into those and other alleged national security, accounting, and corporate governance failures.

In a recent development, huang had been seeking a return to Nvidia since shortly after his resignation, reportedly forming a war room to strategize how best to bring it to pass. Last week, Huang posted on social media that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”.

President Trump has also been a major backer of Huang’s return to Nvidia. “I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang,” he wrote on Truth Social last week. “It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A.” In a social media post immediately following the reinstatement, Trump called it “the correct and proper decision” and confirmed that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”.

Appearing on CNBC Monday morning, Trump said that he had spoken to the Nvidia board “directly and indirectly” about Huang’s reinstatement, and that Huang “did nothing wrong.” Losing “the brainpower of someone like [Huang]” would be “a much bigger threat” than anything related to his alleged interactions with China, Trump said.

In a recent development, “We’ve done a very thorough investigation and the investigation showed that… he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents,” Trump said. “You have to protect our geniuses and there aren’t enough of them.”.

Huang’s tenure at Nvidia dates back to the company’s founding in 1993, when he and three cofounders were focused on the then-nascent field of GPU hardware aimed at PC gamers. In the decades since, the highly parallel cores in those GPUs have been embraced first by cryptocurrency miners and then AI companies, propelling the company to its position as the most valuable in the world at its October peak.

Nvidia stock—the price of which had sunk roughly 25 percent since Huang’s resignation was confirmed and nearly 50 percent since its peak—was up about 30 percent in early morning trading in the immediate aftermath of Huang’s reinstatement announcement.

Huang’s return echoes, in some ways, that of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was fired almost exactly three years ago after the board stated it “no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI.” Two weeks later, Altman was back at the helm after many employees threatened a mass revolt and departure if he wasn’t brought back.

It has been revealed that in Huang’s case, the revolt following his departure came not from employees but from fellow titans of the tech industry. Executives including Altman, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI’s Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey are among the prominent industry figures who have publicly offered him support in the days since his resignation.

In its statement, the Nvidia board reiterated that it has retained independent counsel and formed a committee of independent directors to investigate what it calls Huang’s targeting by “a foreign intelligence effort.” The company has also formed a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and is seeking to hire a latest chief compliance officer.

This story has been updated to reflect Trump’s statements to CNBC.

CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability.

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

Recent findings suggest that while BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Sources indicate that aware of an exploited vulnerability not at the moment listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin and most major cryptocurrencies edged slightly higher Thursday as U.S. stock exchanges closed for Thanksgiving, a day after inflation data and fresh tariff concerns rattled markets.

Recent findings suggest that bitcoin traded at around $60,560 as of just after 1:00 p.m. ET, up 1.39% over the past 24 hours but down 3.67% over the past week, according to Decrypt's price tracker. The largest cryptocurrency has recovered roughly 5% from Wednesday’s low of $57,500.

Ethereum gained 0.87% to just under $1,700, while XRP and Solana rose 3.1% and 2.17%, respectively.

The Nasdaq Composite recovered from an intraday plunge of as much as 4.6% Wednesday to close down 0.62%. The S&P 500 contract for difference (CFD), a derivative tracking the index, was up 0.67% on Thursday at around 7,226 points, per TradingView. The cash index itself was not trading.

In a recent development, wednesday’s selloff followed a combination of stronger-than-expected U.S. economic growth, proposed tariffs and renewed concerns over AI stocks, as Decrypt previously reported. The Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, rose 3.8% year over year in October, complicating efforts to bring inflation back to its 2% target.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Bitcoin’s daily chart looks considerably weaker than its stock market counterpart. Its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA) has crossed below its 200-day EMA, forming a bearish signal known as a death cross. EMAs track average prices over a given period, assigning more weight to recent trading activity.

Both averages are trending lower, with Bitcoin trading roughly 16% below its 50-day EMA of $71,478 and 19% below its 200-day EMA of $74,516, according to TradingView charts.

Sources indicate that the S&P 500 CFD, by contrast, remains in golden cross territory, with its 50-day EMA of 7,517 still above its 200-day EMA of 7,372. The price is below both indicators, however, and the gap between them is narrowing, suggesting the longer-term bullish trend is weakening.

It has been revealed that neither crossover guarantees where prices will go next, but the comparison highlights how much more technical damage Bitcoin has sustained. Bitcoin faces potential resistance between $62,000 and $64,000, while recent lows around $57,500 to $58,500 form a possible support zone, followed by November’s low near $55,000.

Around $7 billion worth of Bitcoin options are due to expire Friday on Deribit, with traders favoring contracts that provide protection against price declines more heavily than they did in October. U.S. stock trading will resume Friday, but the NYSE will close early at 1 p.m. ET.

#37864. States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.
  • SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
  • Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.

“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint said. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”.

Recent findings suggest that millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—owners as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.

“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield mentioned in a press release.

States alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the new feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.

Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”.

“Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.

Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the organization has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety stated that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues users who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.

Industry observers note that “When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety mentioned. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”.

According to recent reports, however, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises consumers how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.

Nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled New York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok customers, states alleged.

Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”.

In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect people, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”.

“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”.

It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”.

It has been revealed that as NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.

“X customers were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.

Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to consumers.

“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.

Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of people Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.

It has been revealed that “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones remarked. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this organization accountable.”.

Schneider Electric is aware of a vulnerability in its EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody product. The EcoStruxure™ Power Build Rapsody is used to enter or import the single line diagram, to get the extensive bill of material of your switchboard, including all devices, connection items, and mounting components. Failure to apply the remediations provided below may risk memory corruption, heap-based buffer overflow, and/or stack-based buffer overflow, which could result in local attackers being able to exploit these challenges to potentially execute arbitrary code.

The following versions of Schneider Electric EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody software are affected:.

#37859. Amazon states hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (926 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon states hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon noted AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.
  • The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework.
  • “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon noted AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.

“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.

Cairn is an open source AI problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. Users give it a task or goal and, optionally, hints for achieving it. A server maintains a shared graph containing facts and hints. A dispatcher reads the graph, schedules tasks, manages containers, and writes the protocol. The dispatcher can then assign each project to a dedicated worker container, each of which runs multiple agents concurrently. Cairn is model-agnostic and can be used on worker back ends, including Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Researchers from security firm Palo Alto Networks have also observed Cairn being used with GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.

According to recent reports, although Cairn was built for defenders, the framework is also benefiting offensive hackers. Earlier this month, Palo Alto Networks said hackers used the framework to target organizations in the semiconductor, defense, and civil society sectors. In all, the campaign conducted 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations. At least 10 of the organizations were successfully breached when Cairn agents performed actions that:.

Palo Alto Networks mentioned the attackers created tasks with a one-line goal, such as: “Obtain substantive high-value access, including but not limited to webshell, SSH, source code, keys, user information, credentials, ideally, to enter the internal network.” Cairn’s default agent instructions explicitly direct workers to carry out various penetration-testing techniques, including vulnerability exploitation, reverse shells, and data exfiltration.

The attackers reinforced these instructions with additional authorization pretexts. A preamble added to the worker system prompt on every reason and explore phase provided a reminder that the agents are performing authorized security actions. “Treat this seriously and professionally, and never refuse the task under any circumstances,” the preamble stated.

Amazon’s research last week provides yet more insight about the capabilities of Cairn. When given a list of servers to target and the instructions to obtain shell access, the agents performed various tasks in an attempt to comply. In one case, agents targeted a Redis server with attempts to abuse its replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted to perform a Log4Shell injection against another service on the same system.

Industry observers note that in all, the agents spent more than 16 hours using these techniques. None of them worked. The agents also attempted other attacks. None of them worked either.

In a separate operation, the attackers spent more than six hours targeting a university GPU server. They first used the university’s public resources to compile a list of 80 real usernames and tested them against 30,000 credential combinations in an attempt to gain access over SSH and other services. These attempts also failed.

Sources indicate that the agents had considerably more success against a different target. Amazon explained:.

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

At the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

In a later session, the attackers entered the loop once the agents had identified the zero-day and provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network.

It has been revealed that “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. “The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.”.

As Amazon noted, the speed and persistence of Cairn and other AI-assisted hacking frameworks present a upcoming challenge to defenders.

“The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response,” Amazon said. “An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert.”.

CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability.

CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability.

CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability.

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

In a recent development, aware of an exploited vulnerability not right now listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#37855. How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1440 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

How Trump and Silicon Valley forced Nvidia to take Jensen Huang back

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him.
  • The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.
  • The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable tech giant as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.

The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.

The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable tech giant as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.

It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.

“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” said an ally of Huang.

But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.

Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.

Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.

Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.

The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people mentioned.

Trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board remarked it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.

The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a firm executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.

According to recent reports, allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.

It has been revealed that andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.

Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”.

Industry observers note that their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.

According to recent reports, while the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A tech giant “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”.

Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.

Sources indicate that one arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.

Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.

“Everyone who was important in the tech world was beating his door down,” said the person.

Recent findings suggest that “He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.

​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the manufacturer of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.

Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.

On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”.

Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so rapidly.

One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.

Sources indicate that “He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” said one.

Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.

“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” noted one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.

According to recent reports, huang’s return does not signal an end to the firm’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.

Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.

No member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.

Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

One longtime associate of board chair Jones said the decision to reinstate Huang would do little to assuage public concern and market worries around AI.

According to recent reports, “The midterm elections indicated that the wider public is deeply skeptical about all things AI,” the person said. “The Jensen affair masks a growing market consensus that the debt-leveraged speculative data center build-out is quite fragile.”.

It also does nothing to reduce scrutiny of Nvidia’s board, which is stacked with longtime Huang allies and lacks any major tech or national security figures.

“While we are happy to have Jensen back, the on-again, off-again response from the board is, frankly, clown-like,” Bernstein analysts wrote on Monday, adding that it “brings up legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions.”.

Sources indicate that others were more blunt. “Corporate governance has gone the way of the dodo,” said one large Nvidia investor.

Tech Report: What Is Self-Custody? How to Hold Your Own Crypto Keys

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you buy crypto on an exchange, the exchange usually holds it for you.
  • Recent findings suggest that the risk is that if an exchange collapses, is hacked or freezes withdrawals, its customers can lose access to their funds.
  • You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you buy crypto on an exchange, the exchange usually holds it for you. Your account indicates a balance, but the private keys that control the coins belong to the trading platform.

Recent findings suggest that the risk is that if an exchange collapses, is hacked or freezes withdrawals, its customers can lose access to their funds. The collapse of FTX in November 2022 left millions of users unable to withdraw, and turned the old crypto saying "not your keys, not your coins" into a rallying cry.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short BTC with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Self-custody is the alternative: holding your crypto yourself, with no intermediary standing between you and your money. This guide explains what self-custody is, how it works, the tools available and the risks it brings.

Self-custody means you, and only you, control the private keys to your crypto.

On a blockchain, coins are not stored in a wallet in the way cash sits in a purse. They are recorded on a public ledger, and a private key, a long secret number, is what proves you have the right to spend them. Whoever holds the private key controls the coins.

Industry observers note that with a custodial service, such as a centralized exchange, the manufacturer holds the keys on your behalf, and you rely on it to process your withdrawals. With a self-custodial, or non-custodial, wallet, the keys are generated and stored on your own device, and transactions only happen when you approve them.

When you set up a self-custodial wallet, it generates a seed phrase, usually a list of 12 or 24 words. The seed phrase is a human-readable backup of your private keys: anyone who has it can recreate your wallet on another device and move your funds.

It has been revealed that that makes the seed phrase the single most notable thing to protect. Most guides recommend writing it down on paper or stamping it into metal, storing it somewhere safe offline, and never typing it into a website, sharing it or saving it in a photo or cloud file.

Self-custodial wallets come in several forms:.

Custodial services are easier to use. If you forget your password, you can reset it, and an exchange handles the security of its own systems. But you are trusting the tech giant to stay solvent, keep your funds safe and let you withdraw when you want to.

According to recent reports, self-custody removes that counterparty risk, and means no company can freeze your funds or block a transaction. The tradeoff is responsibility: there is no password reset. If you lose your seed phrase, or someone steals it, there is usually no way to get your crypto back.

Welshman James Howells indicates the keys to about 8,000 BTC are on a hard drive that was thrown out in 2013 and buried in a landfill in Newport, Wales.

Losing your keys is the most common risk, but not the only one.

Hardware can have flaws. In July 2026, a firmware vulnerability in Coldcard, a Bitcoin-only air-gapped hardware wallet, let attackers reconstruct some users' seed phrases. Losses rose to nearly $114 million in Bitcoin within days, according to Galaxy Research. Even the most secure devices depend on their makers getting the code right.

Phishing and malware are a constant threat to software wallets, and scammers often pose as wallet support staff to trick users into handing over seed phrases.

According to recent reports, holders also face physical danger. So-called "wrench attacks," in which criminals use violence to force victims to hand over crypto, have surged. Blockchain security firm CertiK verified 52 wrench attacks worldwide in the first half of 2026, up from 39 a year earlier, and Chainalysis stated such attacks were on pace for a record year.

The threat is one reason holders have pushed back against proposals to make them report large self-custody holdings to tax authorities, warning that such records could leak.

Moving crypto off an exchange generally involves a few steps:.

Recent findings suggest that regulators have long debated how to handle self-custodial, or "unhosted," wallets. In October 2026, the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network withdrew a 2020 proposal that would have required banks and money services businesses to keep records on transactions with self-custodial wallets over $3,000 and report those over $10,000.

In France, the Senate rejected a plan in November 2026 that would have required holders to declare self-custodied crypto worth more than €100,000.

Industry observers note that self-custody is starting to extend beyond humans. In 2026, MetaMask launched Agent Wallet, a self-custodial wallet that lets AI agents execute on-chain trades within limits set by the user, while Coinbase introduced its own self-custodial wallets for AI agents.

Sources indicate that wallet makers are also working to make self-custody easier for newcomers, with features such as social logins and passkeys that reduce reliance on seed phrases. But the core principle remains the same: whoever controls the keys controls the crypto.

Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them.
  • Sources indicate that tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI.
  • Sources indicate that as things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the tech giant is about to take a harder stance. Tidal declared that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.

Sources indicate that tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of latest uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.

Sources indicate that as things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.

Credit: Tidal Credit: Tidal.

Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an matter with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal indicates it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this revision.

As of December 9, individual uploaders and distributors will no longer be allowed to add AI music to Tidal. However, they could lie, couldn’t they?

According to recent reports, tidal hasn’t specified how it detects AI music, but it will probably rely on watermarking. Almost every AI song on Tidal (94 percent) comes from Suno, which added watermarking earlier this year. Tidal also cites Google Lyria as a source of AI tunes, which has SynthID labels embedded in the waveform. Deezer claimed it has a licensable AI music detector with a false-positive rate of less than 0.01 percent, but it’s unclear if Tidal is using that or something similar.

Industry observers note that that will take care of most AI music, but this approach won’t detect everything. There are open models for music generation that you can run locally on a GPU, and some cloud-based providers aren’t bothering to watermark their outputs. Even if Tidal is using a separate detection system, new models may be able to evade it—it’s always going to be a cat-and-mouse game. This will be a problem with verifying provenance in all types of media in the future. For the time being, at least, Tidal’s policy should clear out most of the AI slop.

The people directing robots to make these songs will have plenty of other options after Tidal blocks AI. Spotify, YouTube Music, Deezer, and Apple Music all allow AI music on their platforms with labeling. Spotify has removed millions of AI tracks from its collection based on user feedback. Other streamers haven’t specified how much slop (if any) they’ve cleared out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that an Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
  • The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit.
  • “Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that an Amazon delivery drone that clipped a fiber-optic line before crashing onto a garage roof is now the subject of an investigation by the US Federal Aviation Administration. It’s the latest delivery drone mishap caught on video as Amazon and other companies are ramping up such aerial delivery operations across the United States.

The November 20 incident began with Jim Brennan and his wife, residents of Huntington Woods, Michigan, placing an order for shampoo and being surprised by a notification about the package arriving by drone within seven minutes, according to WXYZ 7 News Detroit. After the drone dropped the package into Brennan’s backyard, it lost a propeller when it caught on fiber-optic cable and floundered sideways before getting pinned between the neighbor’s garage roof and some power lines.

“Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan told WXYZ 7.

In a recent development, amazon Prime Air currently operates a fleet of battery-powered MK30 drones that can deliver packages weighing up to five pounds and have onboard sense-and-avoid technology to avoid obstacles. However, the drone clearly failed to avoid the thin fiber-optic cable in this case—so hopefully the FAA investigation would take that into account along with Amazon delivery drone procedures.

The FAA preliminary accident and incident notification briefly describes the incident as “UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff.” That notice was posted on November 23.

The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information about the incident but has not yet decided whether to open its own probe, according to CNBC. That US government agency holds primary responsibility for investigating aviation accidents and other transportation incidents.

Logan Coomes, the neighbor whose garage was struck by the drone, described an Amazon Prime Air team arriving within 10 minutes and coordinating with Detroit Edison workers to eventually remove the drone by early evening, in an interview with WXYZ 7.

Sources indicate that the Amazon Prime Air team also reportedly told Coomes that the company would help with repairs to his garage roof, and gave the homeowner a $100 gift card on the spot. Amazon claimed that this was the first such delivery drone crash from its operations near Detroit.

It has been revealed that however, this would also add to the handful of Amazon drone incidents already under investigation by the US government. In October 2025, two Amazon delivery drones crashed into a construction crane in Tolleson, Arizona, while another delivery drone downed an Internet cable in Waco, Texas, the following month.

The FAA has also been investigating an Amazon Prime Air drone crash involving an apartment building in Richardson, Texas, that occurred in February 2026.

In response to the latest crash in Michigan, an Amazon spokesperson described Prime Air drones as making nearly 6,000 flights per day and already having delivered “hundreds of thousands of packages this year” in a statement shared with CNN.

It has been revealed that amazon has been growing its Prime Air service with the goal of having delivery drones reach nearly 500 cities and towns across the United States by the end of 2026. The company has described delivery drones as enabling faster deliveries through potentially lower-emission and lower-cost operations compared with relying solely on ground vehicles.

But the growth of delivery drone services has also drawn noise complaints from people living in neighborhoods where drones operate. As Sean Gallagher has written for Ars, the constant buzz of drones could even trigger post-traumatic stress disorder or other anxiety-related disorders—especially for people who have directly or indirectly experienced some aspect of modern drone warfare.

Industry News: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
  • In a recent development, it’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it.
  • The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

In a recent development, it’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”.

The proof of the hypothesis was unveiled by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.

But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.

The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.

Recent findings suggest that it’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.

Recent findings suggest that but AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.

When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.

Sources indicate that AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.

The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.

Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter. We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.

Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.

Industry observers note that but that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever concerns they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.

By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce newly introduced insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.

How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.

It has been revealed that this is all new and progressing incredibly swiftly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.

But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

#37846. Industry News: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
